item.title: PM clarifies housing issues
item.description: THE Fiji Sugar Corporation will have to develop its own program to replace or renew run-down staff quarters in the North, says Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka. The Prime Minister was told of concerns raised over the condition of accommodation provided for FSC workers.
item.content:encoded:
THE Fiji Sugar Corporation will have to develop its own program to replace or renew run-down staff quarters in the North, says Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka.

The Prime Minister was told of concerns raised over the condition of accommodation provided for FSC workers.

He said the responsibility for addressing the condition of the quarters rested with FSC.

“They will have to come up with their program of replacement or renewal.”

The issue was raised during questions following Mr Rabuka’s tour of the Labasa mill, where staff highlighted several challenges facing the facility.

The condition of staff accommodation has been a concern for workers, particularly in areas where FSC continues to rely on skilled employees to operate the mill.

His comments indicated that any program to upgrade or replace the quarters would need to be developed and implemented by FSC.

The Government has been examining the wider challenges facing the sugar industry, including infrastructure, staffing and the condition of milling facilities.

The issue of accommodation is particularly relevant as the industry attempts to attract and retain skilled workers.

Mr Rabuka has acknowledged that trained workers are drawn to other employers offering better pay.

Improved staff facilities could therefore form part of wider efforts by FSC to retain workers and maintain its workforce in the North, he said.

item.title: Growers council elections’ soon’
item.description: Sugarcane growers could soon elect representatives for the first time in more than two decades following amendments to its governing legislation, the Sugar Cane Growers Council says. Its chief executive officer Vimal Dutt told the Standing Committee on the Sugar Industry consultation that elections could be held once the necessary preparations and funding were in place.
item.content:encoded:
Sugarcane growers could soon elect representatives for the first time in more than two decades following amendments to its governing legislation, the Sugar Cane Growers Council says.

Its chief executive officer Vimal Dutt told the Standing Committee on the Sugar Industry consultation that elections could be held once the necessary preparations and funding were in place.

His comments came in response to Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica, who questioned why elections could not be conducted immediately if the legislative changes had already been made.

“If the laws have been changed, why can’t we have elections tomorrow?” Mr Kamikamica had asked.

In reply Mr Dutt said while the legal framework was now in place, several administrative requirements still needed to be completed before polling could proceed.

He said the amended legislation provided for the Sugar Industry Tribunal and the municipal commissioner to supervise the elections, with the tribunal responsible for conducting the process.

“There are other areas they may need to work on,” he said.

Mr Dutt also revealed that the council had made submissions seeking funding for the elections, but no allocation was provided for this in the recent national budget.

Despite this, he said, the consultations marked positive progress towards restoring grower representation.

He said holding elections would allow cane farmers to choose representatives to serve on the council’s board and advocate on issues affecting the sugar industry.

The last Sugar Cane Growers Council election was held in 2004, leaving growers without elected representatives for more than 20 years.

item.title: Pharmaceutical Society defends Act repeal

item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Pharmaceutical Society (FPS) has defended its support for the repeal of the Registration of Skilled Professionals Act (RSPA), saying there is no evidence linking the legislation’s repeal to pharmacist shortages and insisting patient safety must remain the profession’s top priority.

In a position statement released in response to recent public debate, the Society said discussion surrounding the issue should be based on facts, legislation and evidence rather than assumptions.

“Recent commentary has suggested that the repeal of the Registration of Skilled Professionals (RSPA) Act is responsible for pharmacist shortages in Fiji. No evidence has been presented to establish such a causal relationship,” the Society said.

It argued that workforce shortages cannot be attributed to a single legislative change without considering factors such as graduate numbers, vacancies, workforce distribution, working conditions and market trends.

The Society said it has never opposed overseas-trained pharmacists working in Fiji but maintained that all pharmacists, regardless of where they obtained their qualifications, must meet the same competency standards before treating patients.

“Our position has always been that every pharmacist, regardless of where they obtained their qualification, should demonstrate the same level of competence before being entrusted with the care of Fijian patients.”

It said the Fiji Pharmacy Profession Board remains the statutory authority responsible for assessing whether applicants are qualified and competent to practise pharmacy.

The Society also rejected suggestions that changes introduced under the Registration of Skilled Professionals Act improved access to pharmacy services in rural and maritime communities.

It noted that despite overseas pharmacists being able to enter Fiji through the SPEC pathway since 2016, and pharmacy ownership rules being relaxed in 2022, no new pharmacies were established in locations such as Taveuni or Levuka.

“This demonstrates an important point: the absence of pharmacy services in rural and maritime Fiji has never been a registration issue.”

“It is solely dependent upon pharmacy owners and standard business considerations accounting population size, business viability, staffing availability, logistics and operating costs.”

The Society said decisions on where pharmacies are established remain commercial decisions made by private business owners rather than professional registration bodies.

Defending its support for repealing the legislation, the Society said professional registration should remain solely the responsibility of the profession’s statutory regulator.

“It is imperative to highlight that workforce needs and professional competence are not the same thing.”

“A country may need more pharmacists, but that need cannot replace an independent assessment of whether an individual possesses the competence to practise safely.”

The Society also disputed claims that only three pharmacists were successfully registered in 2025.

It said more than 20 pharmacists were successfully registered during the year, describing it as “possibly representing the highest annual number of pharmacist registrations recorded in Fiji.”

The Fiji Pharmaceutical Society said its position reflects fairness, consistency and, most importantly, patient safety, while calling for public discussion on the issue to remain evidence-based.

item.title: Counter checks for pharmacies
item.description: The Ministry of Health is moving to strengthen enforcement within Fiji’s pharmacy sector, with individuals impersonating pharmacists or providing services without proper registration facing possible action. Principal Pharmacist Inspectorate Reenal Chand said the review of Fiji’s pharmacy laws would address concerns identified in the sector and ensure members of the public received professional ser
item.content:encoded:
The Ministry of Health is moving to strengthen enforcement within Fiji’s pharmacy sector, with individuals impersonating pharmacists or providing services without proper registration facing possible action.

Principal Pharmacist Inspectorate Reenal Chand said the review of Fiji’s pharmacy laws would address concerns identified in the sector and ensure members of the public received professional services from registered pharmacists.

His comments follow reports of pharmacists being absent from pharmacy counters for long periods while assistants attended to customers.

“It is the right of the public to be served by a registered pharmacist when they go out to a community pharmacy or retail pharmacy,” Mr Chand said.

He said while current laws provided the necessary provisions, stronger enforcement was needed to ensure compliance.

“From the recent reporting, such things are happening, so we wish to discourage those kinds of behaviours through better enforcement.”

Mr Chand said pharmacies must display key documents, including the pharmacist’s registration status, pharmacy ownership licence and approval of the premises.

He said the ministry had increased monitoring through regular inspections to ensure pharmacies met legal requirements.

Members of the public were encouraged to confirm that they were being served by registered pharmacists and report suspected breaches to the Pharmacy Profession Board or the Fijian Competition and Consumer Commission.

item.title: Bids sought for hospital project
item.description: The India-funded 100-bed super-specialty hospital project in Fiji is moving closer to construction with shortlisted companies set to arrive this month for site assessments as preparations continue for a groundbreaking early next year. Indian High Commissioner to Fiji Suneet Mehta said the project was progressing well with the tendering process underway for what will be India’s largest grant assist
item.content:encoded:
The India-funded 100-bed super-specialty hospital project in Fiji is moving closer to construction with shortlisted companies set to arrive this month for site assessments as preparations continue for a groundbreaking early next year.

Indian High Commissioner to Fiji Suneet Mehta said the project was progressing well with the tendering process underway for what will be India’s largest grant assistance project in the Pacific region.

He said shortlisted companies would visit Fiji to assess the site, understand the requirements and engage with relevant stakeholders before submitting their bids.

“We expect the team of shortlisted companies to come over to Fiji to do a site visit, understand the lay of the land, interact with all the relevant stakeholders over here,” Mr Mehta said.

He said the visits would help companies prepare their bids, with the selection process expected to move forward soon to allow preparations for the groundbreaking.

“We will hopefully shortlist a bidder soon so that they can start preparations for the groundbreaking to be held by early next year.”

The hospital will be built in Nasinu on land already earmarked for the project and is expected to strengthen Fiji’s healthcare infrastructure.

Mr Mehta said the facility would bring expertise from India through doctors, nurses, equipment and medicines to provide world-class healthcare services in Fiji.

item.title: Hibiscus hopefuls unveiled
item.description: TWELVE women have been unveiled as contestants for the 2026 FMF Hibiscus Festival, marking the beginning of this year’s journey toward the festival crown. The contestants include students, youth leaders, advocates, a journalist and a medical imaging student, each bringing their own experiences and community causes to the annual festival.
item.content:encoded:
TWELVE women have been unveiled as contestants for the 2026 FMF Hibiscus Festival, marking the beginning of this year’s journey toward the festival crown.

The contestants include students, youth leaders, advocates, a journalist and a medical imaging student, each bringing their own experiences and community causes to the annual festival.

Among them are Bulou Boteiova, a Yasawa-born educator and former Miss Coral Coast; Olivia Luisa Gade, a vibrant and faith-driven young professional; Kali Maria Shaw, a medical student promoting health awareness; and Leona Douglas, a political science student advocating for women’s health and youth development.

Also joining the lineup are Temalesi Vakalawa Alutakua, a youth leader focused on mental health support; Nicole Matavesi, Fiji’s Youth Prime Minister; Keren Koroi, a mental health advocate; and Potaisia Rokowailoa, a medical imaging student who champions inclusive communities and challenges stigma through collective support.

Completing the field are journalist Suliana Elizabeth Latianara, youth advocate Sala Korosaya, environmental advocate Salanieta Sekiseki and Emi Ravela, a law student passionate about women’s empowerment and girls’ education.

The 12 contestants will now begin their FMF Hibiscus Festival journey, representing a wide range of professions, experiences and causes while competing for the 2026 Hibiscus crown.

item.title: Ban review every 6 months
item.description: THE ban on the movement of fresh produce from the Yasawa and Mamanuca groups is reviewed every six months, says Commissioner Western Apolosi Lewaqai. Authorities are working with the Biosecurity Authority of Fiji (BAF), Ministry of Agriculture, Fiji Police Force and maritime operators to enforce the restrictions through inspections, public awareness and monitoring, Mr Lewaqai said.
item.content:encoded:
THE ban on the movement of fresh produce from the Yasawa and Mamanuca groups is reviewed every six months, says Commissioner Western Apolosi Lewaqai.

Authorities are working with the Biosecurity Authority of Fiji (BAF), Ministry of Agriculture, Fiji Police Force and maritime operators to enforce the restrictions through inspections, public awareness and monitoring, Mr Lewaqai said.

Yesterday, BAF warned that anyone caught breaching the ban could face a $1000 fine.

The restrictions remain in place to contain the Tongan fruit fly, with the movement of host fruits and vegetables from the Yasawa and Mamanuca groups strictly prohibited.

Meanwhile, the ban has had little impact on fruit and vegetable supplies at the Lautoka market.

Lautoka Market Vendors Association president Filomena O’Neil said most produce sold at the market came from the interior rather than the islands.

item.title: Family hospitalised after fish poisoning
item.description: A FAMILY in Nabua, Suva, was hospitalised after suffering suspected fish poisoning following a Sunday lunch of Ogo. Ruci Cika said several members of her household developed severe symptoms within hours of eating the fish she had prepared.
item.content:encoded:
A FAMILY in Nabua, Suva, was hospitalised after suffering suspected fish poisoning following a Sunday lunch of Ogo.

Ruci Cika said several members of her household developed severe symptoms within hours of eating the fish she had prepared.

“After we ate, around 2 to 3pm, our stomachs started to hurt, including the children. We were vomiting and constantly going to the toilet.”

She said her daughter was among the first to become seriously ill.

“One of my daughters was rushed to CWM Hospital as her case was very serious. After half an hour, I also became very weak in my body, the same with my grandchildren, so all went to the CWM Hospital.”

Ms Cika said other family members later became ill and were taken to the hospital, including her husband.

She said everyone who ate the fish was admitted.

Several other individuals have reported cases of fish poisoning but Assistant Minister for Health Penioni Ravunawa said the ministry was not aware of any reported fish poisoning cases.

He said any verified information would be shared through the ministry’s media channels.

Questions sent to the Ministry of Fisheries remained unanswered.
